title: How does penguin body mass differ across species?
text:
How does body mass differ among Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins? I will compare species summaries and visualize the distributions.
Data come from Palmer Penguins, collected by Kristen Gorman and Palmer Station Antarctica LTER. The data are available under the CC0 licence and included in the R package.
Package citation: Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., and Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3960218.

title: How does penguin body mass differ across species?
text:
Prepare the data
Exclude observations missing body mass or species. Keep the original dataset unchanged.

keep <- !is.na(penguins_data$body_mass_g) &
  !is.na(penguins_data$species)
penguins_clean <- penguins_data[keep, ]
nrow(penguins_clean)

[1] 342

nrow(penguins_data) - nrow(penguins_clean)

[1] 2

title: How does penguin body mass differ across species?
text:
Compare species
Calculate the mean body mass in grams for each species. The counts show how many observations contribute to each group.

table(penguins_clean$species)


   Adelie Chinstrap    Gentoo 
      151        68       123 

mass_summary <- aggregate(
  body_mass_g ~ species,
  data = penguins_clean,
  FUN = mean
)
knitr::kable(
  mass_summary,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Species", "Mean body mass (g)")
)

title: How does penguin body mass differ across species?
text:
Visualize the distributions
A boxplot shows the median and spread, adding information beyond the means.

ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Body mass distributions by penguin species, excluding missing body masses.

title: How does penguin body mass differ across species?
text:
Interpretation
Gentoo penguins had the highest mean body mass at 5076.0 g, compared with 3700.7 g for Adelie and 3733.1 g for Chinstrap. Adelie and Chinstrap had similar means and strongly overlapping body mass distributions. Although Gentoo penguins were heavier on average, the overlapping ranges show that not every Gentoo was heavier than every penguin of the other species.
The analysis retained 342 penguins after excluding two observations with missing body mass. These results describe the sampled penguins and do not establish a causal effect of species on body mass.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Growing up, one of my biggest dreams was to study at a top university and experience life in Canada. Through hard work, dedication, and the different steps in my academic and professional journey, that dream eventually brought me to Vancouver to pursue the Master of Data Science program at the University of British Columbia. I arrived on August 2, 2026, which gave me some time to enjoy the summer and explore places such as Stanley Park, the Vancouver Art Gallery, Kitsilano Beach, and the UBC campus. I have enjoyed how peaceful Vancouver feels, although I quickly discovered that it can also be quite expensive!



Exploring Vancouver before beginning my MDS journey at UBC.


Our MDS orientation began on August 26, and it marked the real beginning of this new chapter. I had already heard that the ten-month program would be intense, but orientation gave me the opportunity to meet my classmates and begin building connections. Although making new friends does not always come easily to me, I enjoy socializing, networking, and helping others, so it was encouraging to meet people at my table and get to know them. Once classes began, I realized that having previous exposure to Python, R, and statistics was helpful, but I would still need a great deal of practice to understand the material deeply and keep up with the pace of the program.
After the first two weeks, I can definitely say that MDS is challenging. There are quizzes to prepare for, labs to complete, concepts to review, and new material arriving constantly. I am learning not only data science, but also how to manage my time, work more efficiently, and ask for support when I need it. I naturally like to take time to analyze problems carefully, so adapting to the speed of the program is something I am actively working on. Some days end with me exhausted and needing a short nap before returning to work, but I keep reminding myself that I worked hard to reach this point and that growth takes persistence. I hope that as the program continues, I will become more comfortable with the pace while continuing to learn, improve, and enjoy this opportunity.

title: Are penguins with longer flippers heavier?
text:
Prepare the data
Remove rows missing a variable needed for the analysis. Keep the original dataset unchanged.

clean = penguins.dropna(
    subset=["species", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]
).copy()
print("Rows retained:", len(clean))
print("Rows excluded:", len(penguins) - len(clean))

Rows retained: 342
Rows excluded: 2

title: Are penguins with longer flippers heavier?
text:
Summarize the relationship
Pearson correlation describes the direction and strength of a linear relationship. Compare the pooled correlation with correlations within each species, because species differences may affect the pooled result.

overall_correlation = clean["flipper_length_mm"].corr(clean["body_mass_g"])
print(f"Overall Pearson correlation: {overall_correlation:.3f}")

for species, group in clean.groupby("species"):
    correlation = group["flipper_length_mm"].corr(group["body_mass_g"])
    print(f"{species}: n={len(group)}, correlation={correlation:.3f}")

Overall Pearson correlation: 0.871
Adelie: n=151, correlation=0.468
Chinstrap: n=68, correlation=0.642
Gentoo: n=123, correlation=0.703

title: Are penguins with longer flippers heavier?
text:
Visualize the relationship
Each point represents one penguin. Colour distinguishes species.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))

for species, group in clean.groupby("species"):
    ax.scatter(
        group["flipper_length_mm"],
        group["body_mass_g"],
        label=species,
        alpha=0.65
    )

ax.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.legend(title="Species")
ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Flipper length and body mass of penguins, coloured by species; observations with missing required values are excluded.

title: Are penguins with longer flippers heavier?
text:
Interpretation
Among the 342 penguins with complete measurements, longer flippers were associated with greater body mass. The overall Pearson correlation was 0.871. Within species, correlations were positive but smaller: 0.468 for Adelie, 0.642 for Chinstrap, and 0.703 for Gentoo.
The scatterplot shows Gentoo penguins generally clustered at longer flipper lengths and greater body masses. The stronger pooled correlation reflects both differences between species and variation within species. These observational results do not establish that longer flippers cause greater body mass. Two observations were excluded because of missing measurements.
